I.	In recent years, artificial intelligence has developed rapidly and transformed many aspects of
governance, society, and global security. However, its implications for authoritarian regimes, especially
in regions with a history of persistent autocratic rule, such as the Middle East, require critical
attention. The very nature of artificial intelligence embodies the duality intrinsic to these technologies:
on one side, the huge potential of AI to drive further innovation, increase efficiency, and reshape a large
number of sectors, from health care to governance; on the other side, its rapid development raises a
large number of ethical, political, and security concerns, especially in authoritarian contexts. The
duality of AI brings opportunities and challenges, as its capabilities may be harnessed for beneficial or
harmful purposes. Within the context of non-democratic regimes, AI could amplify state control,
surveillance, and repression, but it may also enable resistance movements to evade oppressive
measures.
While AI brings with it promises of better governance and economic innovation, its misuse by
authoritarian states has served only to catalyze new forms of control and repression. The Middle East
has been at the intersection of technological adoption with political power for a long time. Traditionally,
the region’s authoritarian governments have relied on surveillance, censorship, and coercion to prop up
their regimes. In the modern era, the technologies of AI, from facial recognition to predictive analytics,
have exponentially enhanced these capacities. The ways in which these tools are employed are not
merely to monitor populations but to suppress dissent and preempt resistance. The ubiquity of AI-
driven surveillance in Iran’s response to protests, Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 reforms, and the UAE’s
Safe City initiatives exemplify the fusion of cutting-edge technology with enduring autocratic practices.

questions.stimulus:
I.	The judicial system, educational system and other infrastructure is the same throughout the country.
On the entertainment front, passion about two pastimes unite Indians more vigorously than anything
else: one is the love for the game of cricket and the other is fondness for Bollywood movies and
associated songs. Unlike the case in the US, there are no frequent messages or new policies about
diversity and inclusivity which only remind us that we are different. Equality is understood at a
fundamental level. Next, let us look at the geographical structure of India from another point of view.
The East has always been the centre of intellectual activities — literature, science, fine arts, economics,
spiritual activities. However, they seem to lack business interest and the drive to accumulate wealth.

They are happy in academic, clerical and various government jobs. When we need people with muscle
(in military, agriculture and various sports, for example) and people who are good looking, especially in
the movie industry, we look at the North.
It was amazing to me to recognize that virtually all famous male Bollywood actors and several
actresses of my time were from Northern India. Although we always knew that South Indians were
exceptionally strong in mathematics, with examples like Ramanujam, the recent explosion in the
number of IT engineers throughout the world coming from the south left no doubt about their superior
analytical skills. The West is where all the rich people are. If you make a list of the top ten wealthiest
persons in India, you will find that most of them are from the three states mentioned above. The
Sensex is in Mumbai; most major banks are headquartered in the west. There are plenty of cross-
fertilizations.www.lawpreptutorial.com
To engage in any profession there is no implicit or explicit requirement that a person must be originally
from that region. Can one learn some lessons from our experience and perhaps build a model for
peaceful coexistence of different nations on this earth? The world has become severely interdependent
in the post-WWII era, primarily because of international trade. While this has led to prosperity, we
have also become vulnerable to conflicts anywhere in the world. This became painfully obvious during

questions.stimulus:
Ill.	Many new electronics goods are built as “disposable products”, observes one repairer, reflecting a
nationwide pattern. The smartphones and slim laptops, in particular, are made so compact that
opening them is difficult. Many customers find it simpler to buy new gadgets than fix the old ones.

waste. As reported in a new study by the UN, e-waste from computers and mobile phones rose 163%
from 2010 to 2022, the fastest growth of any area worldwide. In 2013 alone, Bengaluru produced

second life or every pair of shoes patched up reduces demand for new raw materials and cuts carbon
emissions. One UN-supported programme estimates that formalising e-waste recycling in India will
prevent thousands of tonnes of toxic heavy metals entering the environment and slash about
6,00,000 tonnes of CO2-equivalent emissions.

VI.	India and Japan concluded their 18th Strategic Dialogue in New Delhi, with both sides agreeing to
strengthen cooperation in areas of economic and defence security. The talks were co-chaired by India’s
External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi, and lasted
for over two hours. A major outcome was the decision to establish a Joint Working Group on Critical
Minerals to enhance resilient supply chains, particularly for rare earth elements and other essential
resources critical to advanced technologies and energy transitions. Discussions also covered the
potential transfer of UNICORN radar technology to the Indian Navy, reflecting deepening defence
collaboration.

and initiating a private-sector dialogue to address shared challenges in supply chain stability. Japan’s
focus on diversifying supply chains stems from geopolitical tensions with China, while both countries
emphasized the importance of sustained engagement with partners such as the United States to ensure
regional stability. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The dialogue also reaffirmed the upward trajectory of the India-Japan Special Strategic and Global
Partnership, covering technology, investment, defence, people-to-people ties, and broader multilateral
cooperation, underscoring their shared vision for a stable and resilient Indo-Pacific region.
Source: Keshav Padmanabhan, India, Japan wrap up 18th Strategic Dialogue; talks focus on critical
minerals, UNICORN radar, The Print (Jan. 17, 2026), https://theprint.in/diplomacy /india-japan-

VII. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) has issued an official notification
declaring the area surrounding the Kumbhalgarh Wildlife Sanctuary in the Aravalli mountain range of
Rajasthan as an Eco-Sensitive Zone (ESZ). The notification designates the land from zero to one
kilometre around the sanctuary boundary as an ESZ, aiming to safeguard the region’s fragile ecology
and rich biodiversity. The sanctuary is located across the Udaipur, Pali and Rajsamand districts of
Rajasthan and forms an important part of the Aravalli landscape, known for its dry deciduous forests
and diverse wildlife.
The area hosts several significant species including leopards, striped hyenas, jungle cats, Indian
pangolins, blue bulls, chinkaras, and various bird species such as the painted francolin. The ESZ
notification seeks to regulate and restrict high-impact activities such as commercial mining, polluting
industries, large-scale construction, brick kilns, and similar developments that could harm the
ecosystem. Activities compatible with conservation, including organic farming, agroforestry, eco-
tourism, and sustainable livelihoods for indigenous communities, will be encouraged with appropriate
guidelines.
By establishing this buffer zone, the government aims to balance ecological protection with community-
centred development, strengthening long-term conservation efforts in one of India’s oldest and
ecologically sensitive mountain ranges.
Source: MoEFCC Issues Notification Declaring Kumbhalgarh Wildlife Sanctuary in Aravalli Mountain
Range as Eco-Sensitive Zone, News on Air (Jan. 2026), https:/ /www.newsonair.gov.in/moefcc-issues-
notification-declaring-kumbhalgarh-wildlife-sanctuary-in-aravalli-mountain-range-as-eco-sensitive-
zone/.

declaring the area surrounding the Kumbhalgarh Wildlife Sanctuary in the Aravalli mountain range of
Rajasthan as an Eco-Sensitive Zone (ESZ). The notification designates the land from zero to one
kilometre around the sanctuary boundary as an ESZ, aiming to safeguard the region’s fragile ecology

Rajasthan and forms an important part of the Aravalli landscape, known for its dry deciduous forests

pangolins, blue bulls, chinkaras, and various bird species such as the painted francolin. The ESZ

industries, large-scale construction, brick kilns, and similar developments that could harm the
ecosystem. Activities compatible with conservation, including organic farming, agroforestry, eco-
tourism, and sustainable livelihoods for indigenous communities, will be encouraged with appropriate
guidelines.
By establishing this buffer zone, the government aims to balance ecological protection with community-
centred development, strengthening long-term conservation efforts in one of India’s oldest and
ecologically sensitive mountain ranges.

sustainable diamond trade. India’s leadership in the KP also reflects its prominent role as a global hub
for diamond manufacturing and trade, particularly at a time of shifting geopolitics and heightened
emphasis on responsible sourcing.

indigenous launch capability, further solidifying India’s self-reliance in deploying heavy satellites from
its own soil.

communication satellite CMS-03 for military on November 2.)

questions.stimulus:
XII. Article 21 is considered to be the heart of the Constitution, the most natural and progressive provision
of our living Constitution, the basis of our laws. The purpose of the fundamental right under Article 21
is to prevent the infringement of personal liberty and the deprivation of life except according to the
procedure laid down by law. This clearly indicates that this fundamental right has been established
against state only. The definition of the state encompasses government departments, legislative bodies,
administrative bodies, local authorities that exercise statutory powers, and so on. However, it does not
encompass non-state or private entities that do not have statutory powers. The primary purpose of
Article 21 is to ensure that the procedure laid down by law is followed prior to the deprivation of life or
personal liberty by the state. The right to life is the right to lead a life of dignity and worth. There is no
limit to the meaning of the word life. This right will be available to all the citizens of the country.
Personal liberty is the freedom from physical constraint of the person by the state. It includes all the
types of rights other than the ones laid down in Article 19 of the Constitution. The interpretation of the
right to life today is substantially different from that of 1950 when the Indian Constitution was
enforced. One of the first landmark judgments was A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras where the
Supreme Court absurdly restricted the meaning and scope of personal liberty to just freedom of the
body. The next big case that changed the way we think about the Right to Live was Maneka Gandhi v.
Union of India where the Supreme Court ruled that the word freedom in Article 21 of the Indian
Constitution has the broadest meaning and any law that is passed by the legislature should be in line
with Article 21.

XIV. The doctrine of privity of contract is a fundamental principle in contract law that establishes that only
the parties to a contract have rights and obligations under that contract. This doctrine has its origin in
common law and is now applicable in India and several other countries. Under this doctrine, a contract
cannot confer rights or impose obligations arising under it on any person except the parties to it. The
fundamental rationale underlying the doctrine of privity is based on the interest theory, which states
that only those persons who have an interest in the contract have the recognition in law to protect
them. In other words, only parties to a contract can sue or be sued under its terms. Privity of contract
has three broad effects. First, a third party cannot receive a benefit if he is not a party to that contract.
Second, a third party cannot be held liable under a contract if he is not a party to that contract. Third, a
third party cannot enforce a contract if he is not a party to that contract. The doctrine prevents
strangers to a contract from enforcing contractual obligations even if the contract was made for their
benefit. This principle was firmly established in the landmark case of Tweddle v. Atkinson, where it
was held that a person who is not a party to a contract cannot enforce it, even if the contract was made
for his benefit. However, there are certain exceptions to this rigid rule. These include cases of trust,
contracts for family arrangements, acknowledgment or estoppel, assignment of contracts, and contracts
entered into through an agent. Despite these exceptions, the general rule remains that contractual
rights and obligations are confined to the contracting parties alone.
Source: Jain, Ashutosh (2018). "Doctrine of Privity of Contract Under Indian Law: Should it Be
Abolished in Toto or Subject to Certain Proviso?" SSRN Electronic Journal.

XVII. The girl awakens before dawn, the water in the paddy field shimmering like beaten silver. Her father's
charu kasera, an ornate lounging chair, sits empty on the front verandah. She takes her writing pallet
and sits, feeling her father's ghostly presence in the cane weave. She dips her quill into the inkwell, but
the words for the poem won't come. Instead, she draws a bird, a solitary heron standing on one leg,
waiting.
Four coconut trees on the banks of the lagoon sway, skimming the water before reaching towards the
heavens. The girl bids farewell to the lagoon and the creek. Her uncle, Molayan, had surprised her the
previous day with news of a suitable groom. His tone was insincere, and she felt the pressure of an
impending arrangement. Her mother pleaded with her, "Molay, this is no longer our house. Your
uncle..." Her words trailed off, her eyes darting around nervously.
In the heart of Travancore, South India, a young girl, on the brink of womanhood, lies with her mother
on a mat, their faces wet with tears. The eve of her wedding looms, and her mother shares words of
wisdom, "The saddest day of a girl's life is the day of her wedding. After that, God willing, it gets
better." The girl listens, her heart a heavy stone in her chest, knowing that tomorrow she will be trade d
like a sack of rice, her childhood evaporating into the humid air. She looks at her mother’s hands, rough
from years of labor, and wonders if her own hands will look the same in ten years—worn, tired, an d
empty.
Source: The Covenant of Water by Abraham Verghese (2028)

XVIII. Sooner or later pain becomes too great for fear, and when the people's fear has gone, the regime will
have to go. But for now, the city holds its breath. Eilish stands at the window, watching the rain slick
the pavement, turning the streetlights into blurred stars. The knock on the door had been polite,
terrifyingly so. Two men in dark coats, asking for her husband, Larry. Just a few questions, they said.
That was three days ago.
She looks towards the sky, seeing only darkness, knowing she has been at one with this darkness and
that to stay would be to remain in this dark when she wants for them to live. She touches her son’s
head and she takes Molly’s hands and squeezes them as though saying she will never let go. She says,
to the sea, we must go to the sea, the sea is life. But the sea is miles away, and the checkpoints are
everywhere.
The prophet sings not of the end of the world but of what has been done and what will be done and
what is being done to some but not others. The world is always ending over and over again in one place
but not another. The end of the world is always a local event; it comes to your country and visits your
town and knocks on the door of your house and becomes to others but some distant warning, a brief
report on the news, an echo of events that has passed into folklore. Eilish realizes then that the
catastrophe isn't coming; it is already here, sitting in her living room, drinking her tea, waiting for her
to break.

XIX. Mona said that all of it, the sprints and the ghosting and the three-hour drills, started when our aunt
Ranjan told Pa that what we girls needed was exercise and discipline, and Pa sat quiet and let her tell
him what to do. We were standing in the squash court, the white walls towering over us like the sides
of a glacier. Pa was pacing the gallery above, his footsteps heavy, rhythmic, a metronome counting
down the minutes of our childhood.
Although he is an electrician, the radiators in their home are in poor condition, leading to a cold house.
Gopi believes that in the past, Pa would have solved the problem right away, but now he ignores it. He
misses work appointments, and a character tells the girls he looked lost on the job and left without
having the tea offered to him. Burdened with raising three girls, he confides in a woman about them at
Western Lane—‘Sometimes I look at them and I think they will eat me.’
